Assume first that X is countably compact. Every closed subspace of X is countably compact: if \{U_n\} is a countable open cover of a closed subspace Y, then \{U_n\}\cup\{X\setminus Y\} is a countable open cover of X, and a finite subcover restricts to one of Y.

Let A\subseteq X be infinite. Choose a countably infinite subset B\subseteq A. If B had no limit point, then B would be closed. For each b\in B, choose an open neighborhood U_b such that U_b\cap B=\{b\}. The countable family \{U_b:b\in B\} covers B, but no finite subfamily covers B, contradicting countable compactness of B. Thus B, and hence A, has a limit point. Therefore X is limit point compact.

Conversely, suppose X is limit point compact and T_1. Let \{U_n:n\in\mathbb Z_+\} be a countable open cover of X with no finite subcover. For each n choose
\[
x_n\in X\setminus(U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_n).
\]
The set A=\{x_n:n\in\mathbb Z_+\} is infinite; otherwise, since the cover covers X, all its finitely many points would eventually lie in some finite union U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_N, contradicting the choice of x_n for n\ge N. Let y be a limit point of A. Choose N such that y\in U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_N. Since X is T_1, for each i\le N there is a neighborhood V_i of y with x_i\notin V_i. Then
\[
V=(U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_N)\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^N V_i
\]
is a neighborhood of y. It contains none of the x_i for i\le N by construction, and none of the x_i for i>N because x_i\notin U_1\cup\cdots\cup U_N. This contradicts that y is a limit point of A. Hence every countable open cover has a finite subcover, so X is countably compact.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Assume first that X is countably compact. Let Y be closed in X. Any countable open cover of Y, together with the open set X\setminus Y, forms a countable open cover of X, so Y is countably compact.

Let A be an infinite subset of X, and choose a countably infinite subset B\subseteq A. If B had no limit point, then B would be closed. For each b\in B choose an open neighborhood U_b such that U_b\cap B=\{b\}. The family \{U_b:b\in B\} is a countable open cover of B with no finite subcover, contradicting countable compactness of the closed subspace B. Hence B has a limit point, and that point is also a limit point of A. Thus X is limit point compact.

Conversely, suppose X is limit point compact and T_1. Let \{U_n:n\in\mathbb Z_+\} be a countable open cover of X, and suppose no finite subfamily covers X. For every n choose
\[
x_n\in X\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^nU_k.
\]
The set A=\{x_n:n\in\mathbb Z_+\} is infinite: if it were finite, then because the U_n cover X, all its points would belong to some finite union \bigcup_{k=1}^NU_k, contradicting the choice of x_n for n\ge N. Let y be a limit point of A. Choose N such that y\in\bigcup_{k=1}^NU_k. For each i=1,\ldots,N, the T_1 property provides an open neighborhood V_i of y with x_i\notin V_i. Set
\[
V=\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^NU_k\right)\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^NV_i.
\]
Then V is a neighborhood of y. It contains none of x_1,\ldots,x_N by the choice of the V_i, and it contains none of x_n for n>N because x_n\notin\bigcup_{k=1}^NU_k. Thus V\cap A=\varnothing, contradicting that y is a limit point of A. Therefore every countable open cover has a finite subcover, and X is countably compact.
\end{proof}
